# Classification tree

As an example, here we fit a classification tree, using the pixel based approach.

```{r tree-1, code=readLines("R/models/classification_tree.R"), fold="Classification tree function", message=FALSE}
source("R/models/classification_tree.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

```{r tree-3, code=readLines("R/evaluation/tree.R"), fold="Tree plotting function", message=FALSE}
source("R/evaluation/tree.R", local = TRUE, print.eval = TRUE)
```

We set a seed for repeatability and use five-fold cross-validation. The
complexity parameter is set to `cp = 0.02`.

```{r fit-tree}
set.seed(2023) # for repeatability (generally pick the seed randomly)
tt <- Sys.time() # Measure execution time

## Fit a CART using 5-fold cross-validation to tune the complexity parameter
tree_model <- fit_classification_tree(features_train, y, control, cp = 0.02)
tree_model

## Report execution time
cat("\nExecution time: ", Sys.time() - tt, "\n")
```

The fitted tree shows the pixel splits used to predict each emotion.

```{r show-tree}
## Graphical visualization of the decision tree
options(repr.plot.width = 14, repr.plot.height = 8)
layout(1)
plot_tree(tree_model)

## Textual visualization of the decision tree
tree_model$finalModel
```

The cross validated accuracy estimate is around 55%.

As always, it's useful to check how well the algorithm performs on the training set: If
it doesn't classify the training set accurately, how can you expect better results on
the test set? This seemingly obvious point is often overlooked—surprisingly.

The confusion matrix below measures performance on the training images.
Cross-validation estimates performance on images held out from each fit.

```{r evaluate-tree}
## Check performance on training set
tree_predictions <- predict(tree_model, features_train, type = "raw")
tree_performance <- evaluate_classification(tree_predictions, y)
tree_performance
```
